Relics

History and saints · Theotokos, icons, and saints

Relics

4 sectionsNot completed
Notes

Relics are the bodily remains associated with a saint. The account of St. Polycarp describes the preservation of a martyr’s bones and the remembrance of his martyrdom. St. John of Damascus supplies a theological explanation connecting the saints’ bodies with the indwelling Holy Spirit.[1][2]

How were St. Polycarp’s remains remembered?[1]

The narrative says that Christians gathered St. Polycarp’s bones and placed them in a suitable location. Their gathering there commemorated the anniversary of his martyrdom and remembered those who had already completed their witness. This is a description of the community’s practice in the account.[1]

Read original passage

The Martyrdom of Polycarp: relics

Accordingly, we afterwards took up his bones, as being more precious than the most exquisite jewels, and more purified than gold, and deposited them in a fitting place, whither, being gathered together, as opportunity is allowed us, with joy and rejoicing, the Lord shall grant us to celebrate the anniversary of his martyrdom, both in memory of those who have already finished their course, and for the exercising and preparation of those yet to walk in their steps.

Why does St. John regard saints’ bodies as worthy of honor?[2]

St. John reasons that the saints’ bodies were temples of the Holy Spirit during their lives. He relates the honor given to their remains to God’s presence and power, and describes blessings associated with them. The miraculous claims belong to his theological account and are retained as claims of that source.[2]

Read original passage

John of Damascus: the remains of the saints

Further, that God dwelt even in their bodies in spiritual wise, the Apostle tells us, saying, Know ye not that your bodies are the temples of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you?, and The Lord is that Spirit, and If any one destroy the temple of God, him will God destroy. Surely, then, we must ascribe honour to the living temples of God, the living tabernacles of God. These while they lived stood with confidence before God. The Master Christ made the remains of the saints to be fountains of salvation to us, pouring forth manifold blessings and abounding in oil of sweet fragrance: and let no one disbelieve this. For if water burst in the desert from the steep and solid rock at God’s will and from the jaw-bone of an ass to quench Samson’s thirst, is it incredible that fragrant oil should burst forth from the martyrs’ remains? By no means, at least to those who know the power of God and the honour which He accords His saints.

The martyrdom account’s final chapters[1]

The linked chapters supply the narrative context surrounding the collection and burial of St. Polycarp’s remains. They distinguish this account’s events from the later theological explanation.[1]

St. John’s complete chapter on saints and remains[2]

The full chapter sets St. John’s discussion of relics within his account of honor toward God’s friends. It contains the wider reasoning behind the selected passage.[2]
